summary: Records Differentiated Services working group agreements on new terminology and small technical clarifications, intended to update RFC 2474, RFC 2475 and RFC 2597. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a list of clearer words and fixes for the rules about giving some network traffic priority.

questions: what is an sls and tcs
subtitle: Clarifications for the Diffserv architecture and terminology

tldr.problem: As Diffserv work evolved, terminology needed refinement and technical clarifications became necessary to remove ambiguities in the base RFCs.
tldr.mechanism: This document captures working group agreements on improved terminology (SLS, TCS, PHB Scheduling Classes), clarifies the DS field structure, and addresses confusion around PHB groups and unrecognized DSCPs.
tldr.outcome: Clarifications were incorporated into the revised standards. This informational memo was intended to be obsoleted once its corrections were merged into the updated standards.

facts.label: DS Field bits
facts.value: 6 bits in IPv4 TOS octet / IPv6 Traffic Class

today: RFC 3260 remains an informational document. Its clarifications were intended to be incorporated into revised versions of the standards it updates when those standards progress to Draft Standard status. The terminology it defines is used in Diffserv deployments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: This RFC captures agreements from the Diffserv working group about terminology and small technical clarifications for the Differentiated Services architecture. It updates RFCs 2474, 2475 and 2597 by clarifying definitions that had become ambiguous or contradictory as the work progressed. Rather than recycle the base standards, the working group documented these refinements separately with the intention that they would be incorporated into future revisions of those standards.
sections.eli5: As the team working on Diffserv went along, they found places where the rulebook was unclear or contradictory. Rather than rewrite the whole rulebook, they made a list of fixes.

sections.title: Service Levels and Traffic Conditioning Terminology
sections.content:
The Diffserv architecture used the terms Service Level Agreement (SLA) and Traffic Conditioning Agreement (TCA), but these implied broader business and contractual considerations beyond Diffserv's scope. To clarify, the working group introduced two new terms:

A Service Level Specification (SLS) is the set of parameters that define the service offered to a traffic stream by a Diffserv domain. A Traffic Conditioning Specification (TCS) is the set of parameters that specify classifier rules and traffic profiles. These terms describe only the technical aspects that Diffserv addresses, not the broader agreements.
sections.eli5: When you promise a customer good service, that's a big agreement with many parts. Diffserv handles just the technical part—the rules about how to treat their traffic. The new words separate the technical rules from the business contract.

sections.title: PHB Groups and Instances
sections.content: Per-Hop Behavior (PHB) groups are sets of PHBs that must be specified together because of shared constraints like queue management. The RFC 2597 Assured Forwarding specification defines PHB groups for four independent forwarding classes (AF1, AF2, AF3, AF4), each with three drop precedences. A problem arose from the terminology: RFC 2597 referred to all four classes as a single PHB Group, which contradicted RFC 2475's definition because the four AF classes operate independently of each other. The clarification establishes that Assured Forwarding is a type of PHB group, and each AF class is an instance of that type, not four parts of one group.
sections.eli5: A PHB group is like a set of traffic-handling rules that must work together. But four separate AF classes can work independently, so they should not be called one group. It's like calling four separate kitchens in different restaurants "one kitchen" because they all follow the same recipe—that is not how kitchens work.

sections.title: Definition of the DS Field
sections.content: The DS field is six bits of the IPv4 TOS octet or the IPv6 Traffic Class octet. The remaining two bits were labeled Currently Unused (CU), but after RFC 2474 was published, these bits were assigned to Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), defined in RFC 3168. This created ambiguity: was the DSCP a sub-field of the DS field or an encoding that selects a PHB? The clarification provides precise definitions: the Differentiated Services Field (DSField) is the six significant bits, and the Differentiated Services Codepoint (DSCP) is a value encoded in the DS field that selects the PHB. The two least significant bits are reserved for ECN, not Diffserv.
sections.eli5: A byte in your network packet carries several pieces of information in different bits. Diffserv uses six bits, and the other two are for a different system. The confusion was about what each piece was called.

sections.title: Ordered Aggregates and PHB Scheduling Classes
sections.content: Work on Diffserv support in MPLS revealed the need for a concept to capture sets of Behavior Aggregates (BAs) that share a common ordering constraint. For example, an MPLS router cannot reorder packets of the same microflow if they belong to the same AF class. The clarification defines two related terms: a PHB Scheduling Class is a PHB group for which at least packets from the same microflow must preserve ordering, and an Ordered Aggregate is a set of BAs that share such an ordering constraint. These concepts are essential for routers that apply Diffserv forwarding behaviors.
sections.eli5: Sometimes packets from the same conversation must stay in the same order. These are packets that belong together, and they need to travel as a unit. The new terms describe this grouping.

sections.title: Handling Unknown DSCPs and Edge Cases
sections.content: Implementors found ambiguities about how to handle packets with unrecognized DSCPs. RFC 2475 stated that ingress nodes must condition traffic and either discard unacceptable codepoints or modify them. RFC 2474 stated that interior nodes should forward unrecognized codepoints as if they were marked for the Default PHB. The clarification explains that RFC 2474's language applies at interior nodes (after ingress conditioning), and cross-references RFC 2475 for ingress node behavior. A similar issue arose with Expedited Forwarding (EF) and misconfiguration; RFC 3246 clarified that behavior. These clarifications remove unnecessary confusion and allow flexible implementation.
sections.eli5: What should a router do if it receives a packet with a priority code it does not recognize? Two documents said different things. The clarification explains that it depends on where in the network the router is.
